Mr. WHITE (Leeds) moved the second reading of Bill (JNo. 95) respecting the National Transcontinental railway. He said:	When moving the resolutions preceding the introduction of this Bill, entitled An Act respecting the National Transcontinental Railway, I mentioned all the facts relevant to the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council,, mentioned in the Bill. I also furnished to all members of the House copies of the judgments of tire Supreme Court of Canada and of the Privy Council. I also submitted an estimate showing the liability to date in connection with bond sales that have taken place and an estimate of future liability in connection with bond sales that will be made in the future on the assumption that no higher price will be realized than from the last sale. I assume, therefore, that the House is fairly in possession of all the information they desire. I wish, however, to make it -clear to the public in connection

with this Bill of which I now move the second reading, that the responsibility for this very heavy obligation, in whatever degree such responsibility exists, must belong to the preceding government. So far as this government are concerned, we are merely taking authority under this Bill to discharge the obligation imposed upon the government of Canada by the contract of 1903, entered into between the late government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as interpreted by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. I stated that with regard to bond sales which have taken place the amount of liability under the implementing clause is about $5,000,000, and that a similar sum may be reasonably expected to measure the liability in connection with the sale of future bonds required for the construction of the roiad. The public have been shocked, I think, by the announcement of this very heavy liability. I think the onus is distinctly upon hon. gentlemen opposite, on behalf of the late government, to exculpate themselves, or to extenuate what appears, primia facie, at all exeats, to have been a very great blunder. I reserve any further remarks _ that I have to make in regard to this subject until I hear what explanation is offered by hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with the matter. I beg to move, Mr. Speaker, the second reading of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have no exception whatever to take to the statement which was made by my hon. friend (Mr. White, Leeds), the other day, when he moved the resolution and now in moving the second reading of the Bill, as to the circumstances which have originated and made necessary this legislation. If blame there is to be it ought to attach to the_ parties who were in office when this legislation took place. This legislation is simply an incident of the construction of the Transcontinental railway which was decided upon by the government in the year 1903. When the Bill was presented for the construction of the Transcontinental railway it had not at that time struck everybody, as it struck us, that there was an immediate necessity for the construction of such a highway. On the contrary, it may be said that there was a cleavage of opinion and a good many members of this House and a good many people in the country thought, in good faith, I have no doubt, that the construction of such a railway was, at least, premature. If such an opinion existed at that time, and I quite admit it did exist, I think it has been dispelled long ago. There is no doubt now, I believe, that public opinion is unanimous that the Transcontinental railway which was undertaken in 1903 was an immediate necessity to the rapid development of the 97 J
country and especially to the settlement of the provinces west of Lake Superior. We have evidences more than one of this fact. Indeed, public opinion is *o much reconciled with the idea of having a Transcontinental railway such as was provided for by the legislation of 1903 and. 1904 that, last year, when we introduced legislation into this House for assistance to a further Transcontinental railway, not a single word of objection was hea.u irom anybody. I conclude from this that everybody was agreed then that the action we had taken was in the public interest. We have still at this moment another evidence of the wisdom of the legislation which we put upon the statute-book in the condition of things which exists in the northwestern provinces. We have to-day in the northwestern provinces three different railway systems, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway, every one of them is taxed to its utmost capacity, at the present time they are unable to cope with the requirements of the country and at least one-third if not more of the crop is now lying in the fields awaiting railway transportation. No better justification could be advanced of the necessity under which we were to provide for the immediate wants of the settlers and the wants of the settlers are connected with transportation above all things. Indeed, if we had more railway facilities than we have, if the railways were better equipped with storage capacity and rolling stock, a heavy burden would be lifted from the mind and the heart of the settler at the present time.
But, it was not an easy task to induce any company to enter upon what was, after all, an arduous undertaking, and, it might be, an uncertain one. After negotiating with the Grand Trunk Railway Company they undertook the task of providing for the construction of the Transcontinental railway and the House is familiar with the conditions which were imposed upon us and which have been described by my hon. friend in introducing this motion. In so far as it is necessary for the purpose of the present discussion it may be sufficient to say that in order to induce the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company to undertake the construction of this second transcontinental railway we agreed that upon the western section of the road, from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean, we would undertake to guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to the extent of three-quarters of the cost of the construction of the road, limiting the liability, however, upon the prairie section, to $13,000 a mile and, upon the mountain section, to $30,000 a mile. This agreement was modified, as has been.

shown already by my hon. friend, in the following year and, as I said a moment ago, I have no reason at all to complain of the statement of the hon. gentleman in Introducing the motion because I think he presented the case in a very clear and a very fair manner. I will quote his own words in introducing the motion the other day:
it the time this agreement was entered into, the 3 per cent stock of the Dominion of Canada stood at about par. Shortly afterwards there was a fall in that stock in common with other high class low interestbearing securities, and as a result it was seen that the 3 per cent Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company's bonds guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada would not realize nearly par. In order to meet that situation a supplementary agreement was entered into in the following year. Among other things it removed the limit as to the $30,000 a mile upon the mountain section, but allowed the $13,000 per mile as a maximum of bonds to be issued by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company on the prairie section to stand.
That is a very fair statement of what took place and of the reasons which induced us to make the modification which we made of the agreement of 1903. Shortly after we had introduced the legislation of 1903 the financial' market commenced to decline and declined steadily. It was not supposed, however, that it would be permanent. It was expected that, on the contrary, the financial market would resume its buoyancy and that our securities, which, at the time we entered into the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in 1903, stood at about par and, which had declined would resume their former position. However, in this we have been disappointed as everybody knows. The financial market has been going down steadily ever since, not only in regard to Canadian securities, hut in regard to the best securities in the world. English consols, for instance, which ever since the wars of Napoleon had been the most favoured stock in the financial market, and which, during the later years of the last century, stood not only at par but at a large premium, sometimes ranging as high as 10 per cent, have declined steadily ever since and if I am not mistaken-indeed I am not mistaken-in the month of December English consols went down to 77. I have not looked at the, quotations recently, but I think they have been still declining. So that, if our securities have been declining ever since it is not on account of any want of confidence in our credit, but it is simply on account of the larger demands that have been made on the money market, the result being that the price of money Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
has risen accordingly. Everybody knows that the impetus which has been given to the development of natural securities, especially electrical securities, has been almost phenomenal in the last ten years.
This is regarded as a gilt-edged security, but the price of money ha3 risen on account of the extraordinary demand to meet this new development in the industrial world. Under these circumstances, the value of our securities has been steadily declining. That is the origin of the legislation we passed in 1904, and which we are now about to implement by providing to meet the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, rendered on the agreement which was passed between us and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in 1904. I may say that I acquit the Minister of Finance and the government from all responsibility in this matter; the government in introducing the legislation is simply taking the proper steps to comply with the judgment of the Privy Council. Under the enactment of 1903 we guaranteed three-fourths of the cost of construction of the western section of tlie_ road, limiting our obligation on the prairie section to not more than $13,000 a mile, and limiting our obligation on the Mountain section to not more than $30,000 a mile. The modification we made in that is to be found in section 5 of the Act of 1904, which reads:
Notwithstanding anything in the said contract contained, the government may and shall, preserving always the proportions in the said contract provided as between the Prairie and Mountain sections of the eastern division, implement for the purposes and subject otherwise to tlie provisions of the said contract, its guarantee of the bonds of the said company to be issued for the cost of construction of the said western division, in such manner as may be agreed upon, so as to make the proceeds of the said bonds so to be guaranteed a sum equal to seventy-five per centum of the cost of construction of the western division ascertained as provided in the said contract, but not exceeding in respect of the Prairie section, thirteen thousand dollars ($13,000) per mile.
There were two provisions in this agreement, one, was that the restriction of the liability of the government with regard to the mountain section of $30,000 per mile was removed, and we also undertook to implement the difference between the face value of the bonds and the price they would bring in tlie market. Now, we did this because it became evident that at least some of the bonds which were to be issued from time to time could not realize par or anything like it. We were in hopes that the money market might become more buoyant, and that we would not have very much in the end to make up, but in this our expectations were not realized. The

money market has been steadily declining, and, as the Minister of Finance has very properly said some of them sold at 924 and others sold at only 80, making a great difference between the face value and the selling price. Now, why did we make this arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company?
It seems to us that under such circumstances if the Grand Trunk Pacific company was bound to raise its money at that sacrifice, that its credit and its resources might be impaired, and the enterprise might be jeopardized. We thought on the whole, that it was worth every effort on the part of the Canadian government, on the part of the Canadian parliament, on the part of the Canadian ipeople, to provide for this Transcontinental railway, which would be of such benefit to the settlers of the west, in enabling them to bring their products to the market. We all know that what has contributed most of all to make Canada prosperous, has been the rapi'd settlement of the western prairies, and that the more facilities were given, to the settlers to dispose of their crops the more prosperous they would be, and the more prosperous would be the country as a whole. The government at the time placed itself in the judgment of the House and the House approved our action, and I believe the Canadian ipeople also approved. Even though the cost may be heavy, I do not think it is too heavy for the resources of the country or for the results which have already been achieved, and which still remain to be achieved. The only difficulty that arose in connection with the matter, was as to the interpretation of this agreement, and as to in what manner the implementing should take place. That has been a question between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the government for some years past. I need not tell the House-many of the old members remember it-that when we made the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway company, the government engaged the services of some of the most able counsel who could be obtained. We had the Minister of Justice, who did not himself take any technical part in the framing of the contract, and who left this largely to Mr. Newcombe, the Deputy Minister of Justice, and to one of the most able counsel of the Dominion, Mr. George F. Shepley. These gentlemen prepared the contract for our guidance, and even though our best efforts were given to make it a document that could not be disputed, still, as doctors differ, so will lawyers and judges. When the difficulty arose, Mr. Shepley and Mr. Newcombe advistM us that the proper method of implementing would be to issue bonds, so as to make up the difference, whereas, the Grand Trunk Railway Company took the position that the implementing should be only by the payment of cash to the amount of the difference between the face value of the bonds and the price they realized. Then, the matter was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada. Before I proceed, might I refer to a remark made by my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance a moment ago, when he said that the blame, if blame was to fall upon anybody, must fall upon the previous administration.
I agree altogether with my hon. friend that if blame must fall upon anybody, it must fall upon us. But in such a matter it may well be considered whether or not we are Very much to blame after all. The question was one of law, and let me before I go further, state to the House what was the opinion, as to the construction of the contract which we made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, of a gentleman well versed in law, whose eminent ability as a lawyer is well known; I mean the Deputy Minister of Justice. When the difference arose with the Grand Trunk Railway Company as to the interpretation of this contract, the matter was referred by the Minister of Finance to Mr. Newcombe, and this is the opinion which was given by Mr. Newcombe:
In reply I beg to state that in my opinion that method of implementing is still open to the government. In the first place I think that the whole transaction shows that there was no intention that the government should pay cash otherwise than as expressly provided, and it is my opinion that under the legislation and agreements the government has not the power to pay the deficit in cash as proposed by the company.
Then, section 5 provides that the company is to implement its guarantee ' so as to make the proceeds of the said bonds so to be guaranteed a sum equal to seventy five per centum of the cost of the construction of the western division, ascertained as provided in the said contract but not exceeding in respect of the Prairie section $13,000 per mile.' It will be seen that the method of implementing proposed by the company would not fulfil the object for which the implementing was to be undertaken, that is to say, it would not make the proceeds of the bonds a sum equal to 75 per cent, of the cost of construction, &c., while the other method would comply with this requirement to the letter.
Again, -the recital of the -implementing clause in the mortgage schedule can hardly be taken to have had any other object than to account pro tanto for the amount of the issue to be made under the mortgage, and we know as a matter of fact that there was included in that amount the sum of $1,255,125 in respect of bonds to implement on a basis of 92j per cent.

But when it was pointed out to the right hon. gentleman and his ministers that there was a possibility of such a construction being put upon this clause, and when they had it in their power to amend the clause so as to remove any doubt, why did he not have the clause amended and .save the country $10,000,000?

I have said already that we had the opinion of the hon. member for Hamilton on the one side and that of Mr. Shepley and Mr. Newcombe on the other. Let me again read the opinion' of Mr. Newcombe that in his view the question did not admit of doubt.

Certainly, but he was construing the contract and he said that it did not admit of any doubt. As I have said there is a condition to-day in the Northwest which must cause anxiety, not only to the gentlemen on the treasury benches, but to the whole Canadian people. You have in that country any amount of wheat awaiting transportation for lack of railway accommodation. It is to be hoped that the railway companies will be able to give more storage facilities and provide more cars than they have been able to give hitherto, and in that way mitigate to some extent the condition now prevailing.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the Bill, I

shall perhaps take a little liberty with the House, by going back upon some of the facts, and I may not altogether agree with what the right hon. gentleman has .iust said as to the facts. I think, however, that there can be no question in this House that the Bill introduced by the Minister of Finance, should be supported. I shall do so simply because there is not now any question whether we wisely undertook certain things in 1904, but the sinmle fact that we did enter into a certain undertaking by which the highest court of the empire has decided we have obligated ourselves to pay the money that is asked for. Therefore, Sir, if it was three times the amount involved, there should be no hesitation now, and I trust that as Canadians we shall not allow any question to be raised upon that point. What we have agreed to, what we have undertaken, we will abide by, and I therefore sincerely hope that every member in the House, for the credit of the country, will vote for the Bill.
But, Sir, while doing that, I think we are justified in asking the House to go back upon the history of the transaction which has involved us in this very serious loss of public money. It is due to members on this side of the House, who were then in opposition, and1 to the country which after all, must bear the brunt, that we should look back now and see how this was all brought about, and whether the case is as simple as the right hon. gentleman affects to think it is. If I understand the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition (Sir Wilfrid LaurieT) aright he is under the impression to-day that when this question was first opened in the country, there were a great many people who thought that the construction of the railway was not needed then, that it waS premature. I do not know just what my hon. friend is referring to. If he says that many people thought at that time there was no need for additional railway facilities for the transportation of the grain produce of the great northwest to the ocean, then he is altogether outside the facts. I was in the House at that time and I can vouch for the opinion of every member of the Conservative party; I venture to say, there was not one man on the Conservative side who doubted for a moment the absolute need of another through railway at the earliest possible moment. There were in the Conservative party at that time members who were interested in other railways, some in the Canadian Pacific railway, and others in other roads, but every one _ of them, whether interested in the Canadian Pacific railway or not, agreed that another railway should be built, that the party should unanimously support any generous liberal subsidy the government would propose to give, and that we should facilitate the construction Mr. BARKER.
of the road in every way. That is putting it according to what I know to have been the feeling then on the Conservative side; and so far as my knowledge and observation went, it was the opinion of every man on both sides of the House.
Hon. gentlemen will recollect that in November, 1902, a notice appeared in the ' Canada Gazette ' of an application to parliament for a charter for a company to be called the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. That was the root of this whole matter. I shall read, before concluding, the application of that company to the right hon. (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as Prime Minister of Canada for a subsidy and the conditions they proposed. The application will show 'that they proposed a line from the Pacific ocean at or about Port Simpson to and through Edmonton, and to and through Winnipeg, and then to North Bay. At North Bay their proposed line would have connected with the existing railway system of Ontario, which would have carried the line through from the Pacific to Montreal, where it would meet the Intercolonial owned by the government. Thus by the project proposed to the right hon. gentleman there was offered to us at the earliest possible moment a through line from the Pacific ocean to Halifax, another real transcontinental railway about whose early construction there was very little doubt.
I understood the right hon. gentleman to say that there was a great deal of difficulty in inducing any. company to undertake the construction of such a line. The hon. gentleman had in his own hands that proposition as early as November, 1902, and he did not allow the people of this country or of this House or his followers to know that he had that until two years afterwards. He treated that-paper as a confidential letter and he kept it in his own possession. Yet knowing that he had that he tells the House that it would have been impossible at that time to get any company to undertake the construction of sucn a road. This is not new to us. We have been charged with opposing the Transcontinental railway. We never opposed that system at all. We did not know exactly what the proposal of the Grand Trunk Company was to be for the best reason in the world, that the right hon. gentleman would not let us see it. It was impossible for us to know, we did not know what terms they proposed or what subsidy they expected, but we thought they would ask a good deal more than they expected to get and that the government would have dealt reasonably and liberally with them and no more. So, from every possible point of view, opportunities were presented to the gov-

eminent for the construction of that railway at the earliest possible day.
It was not possible for the proposed company to . do what they desired to do, and what events have shown would have been the very best thing for Canada. In 1903, there were in the city and province of Quebec certain personal and political friends of the right hon. gentleman who had various railway, bridge and other projects and schemes more or less visionary and more or less financially hopeless. After the private Bill of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company had been introduced in the House, it was referred to the Railway Committee. Immediately there were rumours of all kinds. We heard of personal negotiations between the right hon. gentleman and the Grand Trunk railway officials. The right hon. gentleman undertook to negotiate ' off his own bat ' with some of the ablest railway men in the country-did it all himself. When, some weeks afterward, the Bill came up in the Railway Committee-I was present-the right hon. gentleman informed us that he had made another arrangement than that proposed by the Bill. He proposed that the railway should be constructed easterly from Winnipeg towards Lake Abitibi and thence to the city of Quebec. And there was to be a branch from the neighbourhood of Abitibi, to North Bay and a branch to Montreal. This was announced to us as a perfectly new idea. The Grand Trunk railway officials were there, and if I i m any judge of men's countenances, they assented very unwillingly and under pressure. I do not think that any man who saw them could possibly doubt that. The next stage was that another set of men came in. The right hon. gentleman had political and personal friends away down east in New Brunswick. After a week or two, and after further private and personal negotiations-it was said at that time that the right hon. gentleman was meeting the railway officials in private cars, away from the Cabinet and from his ministers; doing the whole thing himself- we had another meeting of the Railway Committee; and we found that the proposed line was to be extended down into New Brunswick, Moncton being ultimately named. And that line as proposed then by the right hon. gentleman paralleled the government's own railway for hundreds of miles. That is not all. The right hon. gentleman had some more friends: he had some friends in Quebec and vicinity, and so it came about that the taking up of the two sections from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton involved taking up that most lamentable affair, the Quebec bridge. And thereupon, as we find, the bridge company was taken over. They had received bonuses from the Dominion
of Canada towards that bridge, from the province of Quebec and from the City of Quebec. They had spent all they had received and were in debt something over $900,000. They were'utterly bankrupt-stranded; their charter was not worth a dollar. But a very prominent Quebec gentleman was at the head of the company, and the next thing we knew the government was buying up this concern. The government took over its liabilities, compensated the shareholders and directors of this bankrupt concern, and it became part, to all intents and purposes, of the great Transcontinental line. It is almost amusing to think that the hon. Mr. Fielding, in 1904, when addressing this House, put the amount at which the bridge should be chargeable to the Transcontinental railway at $2,000,000;-he thought that was excessive, but he generously charged that amount against the bridge. EveTy one who knows the history of that bridge is quite sure that the cost of that part of 'the project will be seven times two million. But in the airy way they had of handling millions in those days, they put it down as $2,000,000. It was perhaps, the most unfortunate ipart of the whole project-though we have not yet, it may be, heal'd all the misfortunes of the eastern division. That bridge, as we all know, dropped into the St. Lawrence, carrying with it scores of poor workmen. We had been paying millions on the bridge and the government had not even insured the payments it made. And the government contract for construction was with a corporation in the United States, the capital of which was $100,000. This was another instance of the business abilities brought to bear upon the construction of this gigantic work. The one visible asset we got from the bridge company was a lawyer, a political and personal friend of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was taken over as supervisor and superintendent of construction of the eastern division of the great Transcontinental line at a handsome salary. We got him, and that is about all we had, I think, for the money the country expended in buying out the old bridge company.
Now, it may be just as well here to consider the difference :in the two propositions. The first is that which tlhe skilful railway men had planned out, a simple undertaking, that would have been profitable to them and most useful and most profitable to the country. The Grand Trunk's proposition was to carry a line from the Pacific to North Bay. That was to be the whole construction. And they would undertake it for certain subsidies to which I shall refer presently,-we did not know what they were then, for the reason I have already stated, but they were a subject for consideration, and no one would have objected to a generous treatment, but not

The right hon. gentleman then dealt wdth. several of the clauses of the 1904 agreement not directly connected with the resolution now before the House, and, therefore, I pass them by at present.
Coming to the change made in section 28, which change was, of course, one of those which would surprise us as to the moderation of the Grand Trunk Company, and which would cause us to be vexed because it deprived us, the opposition, of a good deal of the thunder which we were prepared to fulminate, he proceeds to inform the House that the restriction of the guarantee to $30,000 per mile of the cost of construction of the Mountain section was removed, and that now the government undertook to guarantee 75 per cent of that cost whatever it might be. Then, too, he .said the government undertook to implement the proceeds of the sales of the bonds, so as to make the amount actually going into the construction, 75 per cent of the total cost of construction..
So there was one modest little demand which was to vex us, the vile opposition of that day, from its very moderation. Let us see what it meant to Canada.
The president of the Grand Trunk, addressing his shareholders at a meeting a few weeks previously, had said, on the latest information, that the mountain section -would cost for construction $56,000 a mile. Therefore the government knew that in removing the restriction of $30,000 per mile they were subjecting the * country to a guarantee of $42,000 per mile, or an addition to our obligations on that section of $12,000 per mile, or for, say 500 miles, an increase of $6,000,000 with interest.
Having thus crushed us with .such a trifling concession, the right hon. gentleman proceeded to lay before us another of his little arrangements, but this one, he admitted, in ceirtain possibilities might cost the country a little more. He apparently had not at all realized how much was involved in omitting the restriction to $30,000 a mile.
Well, not content with removing the restriction of one guarantee to $30,000 a mile, he further undertook that the government should implement the guarantee so that the company should receive par for the bonds guaranteed as to both the Mountain and Prairie sections. That might, he admitted, cost us a little more. So far, as you see, it is costing us in round numbers about $10,000,000-and we must not forget that that money is gone forever -not recoverable-and there will be more to follow.
Now, let us see just where we stand as to this $10,000,000. The Finance Minister will of course borrow the $10,000,000 at interest, and hand it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific as a gift. But as we have

guaranteed the bonds to the holders, then if the Grand Trunk Pacific fails to pay, we must pay that money again to the bondholders with interest. And under section 32 of the agreement, -we must, for the first seven years from the date of the 'bonds guaranteed on the Mountain section, pay all the interest to the holders and have no recourse against the Grand Trunk Pacific. And, further, for the next three years, if we pay interest on those guaranteed bonds, we must accept re-payment from the Grand Trunk Pacific not in cash, but in 40 year bonds bearing interest. So that, about 47 years after the date of the bonds, we will get only the three years' interest back.
Now, there was something said by the right lion, gentleman as to their misunderstanding. There was no misunderstanding. The right hon. gentleman knew perfectly -well that there was a question about the meaning of that clause. Does he suppose that if there had been a doubt raised on the side of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company as to its meaning, they would have failed to get it put beyond a question? All that he had to do was to say to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company: There seems to be a doubt as to the meaning of this implementing.
I had pointed out that if the bonds should not realize par, the government must bear the loss, without recourse; and so it would be wiser to require the company to issue additional guaranteed bonds for which the government would only be a surety. But the then Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) said in reply to me:
I have no doubt the hon. gentleman's method would be the best, but I do not think he has any justification for assuming there is going to be a loss on the sale of the bonds. We all hope that the market will improve.
So they preferred to take the risk, and we had the right hon. gentleman and his ministers gambling on the stock market. The right hon. gentleman was inclined to admit that there might be a little more loss in dealing in their methods than there otherwise would have been. He used the expression: ' it might cost a little more.' That was just like the $14,000,000 Quebec bridge which we were told was likely to cost $2,000,000. The cost of everything undertaken by the late government was belittled. Fie knew perfectly well the risk they were taking, yet he would not ask the Grand Trunk railway to insert a few words in its agreement which would have made the meaning clear. The addition of ten woi'ds to that clause would have made its meaning clear beyond question, and every word inserted would have been worth a million dollars to the country.
As I have just made reference to the exMinister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), I
think I ought to read to this House the very words he used in a celebrated statement. We have all heard discussed in the press and on the hustings the $13,000,000 prophecy of Mr. Fielding. He told us that all that railway from Moncton to the Pacific was going to cost Canada would be $13,833,356, and we could pay tha.t out of one year's surplus. Let me read his words. They will be found in the fourth volume of ' Hansard ' of 1902, page 3631, 26th May:- A summary, briefly, of the figures show the following:-	,
Total present sum required to cover 7 years' interest (all other interest being paid by the company) on
cost of eastern division	$10,655,562
Total present sum required to provide government portion of 7 years' interest (all other inter'est being paid by the company) on cost of mountain section, western division	 3,177,791

' That is to say, if out of our large surplus this year, we should set aside $13,833,356, it would provide for the full payment on the seven years' interest which is all the obligation that the government are to bear as respects the whole line from Moncton to the Pacific.'
You will observe that he absolutely ignored the obligation to make good the loss on the sale of bonds, which we then pointed out to him. He was satisfied the market was going to improve and we were not going to lose on the sale of these bonds, and we now have to pay $10,000,000 of a loss; he did not take that possibility into his calculation at all. He just figured out the interest, and told us that $13,833,356 would be the cost to the government of the whole line from Moncton. How many other items did he ignore?
I started out by saying that I would read the original 'proposal of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the late government. That will be found in volume 2 of ' Hansard ', 1904. It is a very important document. It is a document which the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) received before this question came before parliament at all. It is a document that was never produced although time and again the opposition made formal motions in the House for the production of every paper relating to this undertaking. My right hon. friend the then leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) my hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) and several other hon. gentlemen moved again and again for the papers. They called the attention of the right horn, gentleman to the fact that we wanted every paper relating to the subject, and he assured us that the government had brought down' every one. He was most emphatic. He made that statement so unequivocally that the Minister of Public

Works (Mr. Monk), then in opposition withdrew his motion. The right hon. gentleman knew that my hon. friend withdrew his motion on the faith of that assurance. Well, that paper I now propose to read. I should add that when the right hon. gentleman was charged with unfairness, he said that it was a confidential paper, and he did not undertake to produce confidential papers. He called it at other times a confidential letter to himself. Well, here is the document:-
Confidential.
Montreal, Que., Nov. 3, 1902. To the Right Honourable
Sir Wilfrid Laurier, G.C.M.G., P.C., Premier of the Dominion of Canada, Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-Your petitioners desire to memorialize your government in regard to the construction of a first-class line of railway from the northern terminus of the Grand Trunk railway, at, or near, North Bay, Ont., through to the Pacific coast, for the reasons and upon the conditions set forth:
1.	That it is considered very desirable and in the public interest that there should be, without any unnecessary delay, a second transcontinental railway reaching from the Atlantic ocean to the Pacific ocean, in order that additional facilities may he provided for the large growing business of the Northwest, *which might otherwise find its outlet through American channels.
2.	That your petitioners propose, as soon as authorized by your government, to undertake the construction of such a line from North Bay, Ont. (or some other point north thereof, to be defined) to the Pacific coast, the terminus to he at or near Port Simpson, with all necessary branches along the route, to be designated.
3.	That your petitioners, therefore, ask that their application for authority to construct such a line of railway, to he called the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, shall he granted.
That was, of course, a personal application to the right hon. gentleman, for a charter to construct this line.
4.	That your petitioners will he prepared, immediately an agreement is entered into by the government, and the concessions hereinafter mentioned are sanctioned by an order in council, to place a corps of engineers in the field, both at the eastern and western ends and at other points on the projected line.
5.	That the routes to be selected shall he *submitted to and approved by the government, after proper surveys have been made.
6.	That as soon as plans and routes are approved, work shall be commenced and the road shall be completed and in operation within a period of five years from the time the Act is in force.
If the government had passed this Act in 1903 these men were willing to undertake that by 1903 the line would be running throughout.
7.	That all the work shall he subject to the inspection and approval of the chief engineer of the government.
Mr. BARKER,
8.	That in order to provide for the connections with the Atlantic seaboard all the year round and through an all-British territory route, your petitioners will be prepared to enter into an arrangement with the government for an interchange of traffic, or other satisfactory agreement, with the Intercolonial railway at Montreal, or to consider such other proposal as the government may submit.
Will the right hon. gentleman say that that was not a material thing to be laid before parliament when we were discussing this measure? We were contending that under his arrangement it would be possible for the Grand Trunk Pacific railway to divert the traffic to Portland instead of going on to Halifax or St. John.
9.	That your petitioners would have the advantage of all the eastern connections, in Ontario and Quebec, of the Grand Trunk railway, and by this means on the completion of the Transcontinental line there would be established and opened up a complete system from ocean to ocean.	-	[DOT]
10.	That the conditions referred to in clause
4, upon which your petitioners would undertake the carrying out of the proposed work, may be set forth as follows:-	_
(a)	That the Dominion government will grant a cash subsidy to your petitioners of $6,400 per mile of x-ailway, and in addition 5,000 acres of land per mile.
(b)	That the payment for the carriage of the mails shall he calculated on the same basis as provided for under the contract made with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
(c)	That rails and materials of every kind used in the construction of the railway-if dutiable-shall be admitted free, if such material cannot he obtained in Canada upon equally favourable terms.
(d)	That the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and all stations and station grounds, workshops, buildings, yards and other property, rolling stock and appurtenaces required and used for the construction and working thereof, and the capital stock of the company, shall be for ever free from taxation by the Dominion or by any province hereafter to he established "or by any municipal corporation therein; and the lands of the company in the Northwest Territories (until they are either sold or occupied) shall also be free from 6uch taxation, for 20 years after the grant thereof from the Crown.
Your petitioners ask that your government will give the prayer of this petition their early and most earnest consideration.
And your petitioners will ever pray.
On behalf of the petitioners,

At page 3705 ' Hansard ' 1904, the right hon. gentleman, in referring to this paper which I have just read, a most formal petition to him as Prime Minister to be laid before the government, said:
This confidential letter was in my own possession.

I have thus gone over the history of this transaction. I do not wish to discuss the question of the law; that has been settled by the highest court of the empire. If there was a doubt such as the hon. gentleman mentioned, when he was taking the advice of counsel as to what that meant, the simple way was to put it clearly in the agreement and settle the thing altogether. Why did he need to take advice afterwards and then injure, as he must have injured, the credit of this country by trying to get out of the legal obligation he had entered into? It was not creditable to the government of that day or to any government. The matter was clear, they were to make good the proceeds up to 75 per cent. Would it require a lawyer to say what that meant? It is more a question of business. The whole thing was brought to the attention of the minister in 1904, and all he had to do, as I said, was to have ten words added to the agreement and there would have been no trouble. It would not have made any difference because the right hon. gentleman intended to go on with it anyway. Mr. Fielding, the Minister of Finance, was also determined to do it. The right hon. gentleman thought it was going to cost a little more. Mr. Fielding thought that my plan was the better one, but he had hopes that the price of bonds would improve in the market.
The right hon. gentleman made a point of this opening up new country to the north, and he said that some people thought it was too early, that it was premature. That is where the point arose of some pepple thinking the project was premature; they thought it was premature to go through the wilds of the north, but not that the construction of such a railway as the Grand Trunk proposed was premature, everybody agreed on that. What ought to have been done in or since 1904 was for the province of Quebec to do what Ontario is doing, build a railway up in to the territory to the north. They are doing that, and they will in that way open up and develop that northerly country. Quebec should have done the same thing in the country up to the north of the old settled portion of that province. The Dominion might have helped them if necessary, and after they had opened up and de-veloiped the country there so that we would have known positively what there was in that country, it would have been time to build the line east and west. Those people who said the project was premature in this respect were right, and I think the more we have seen of it the more we are convinced of that fact. But the right hon. gentleman preferred being poetic. He spoke of the roses that bloomed away up in the north, and he had other
quotations. He prayed Heaven it was not too late, he must go ahead blindly without surveys or anything else, and, great as the loss has been as we now see on that western division, I very much fear that it is a trifle and will 'be a trifle compared with the exposures wre may expect on the eastern division.
All that we are talking of to-day_ has nothing to do with the eastern division- the government is building that; and we have yet to learn what disclosures are in the right hon. gentleman's possession as to it.
I hope there are no more ' confidential letters,' no more private negotiations. I do not know whether there were any private negotiations about these bonds or in any other respect. But the right hon. gentleman certainly did an extraordinary thing. The Grand Trunk Railway company were allowed to sell these bonds in England. It mattered not to ifhem whether the discount was 10 per cent or 20 per cent, because the government had to make good the loss, and he apparently put it in their power to sell as they pleased on the market. Of course, I do not mean to charge him or the company with dishonesty or any desire for dishonesty; but it was not businesslike of the right hon. gentleman to put that in their hands. It is true, there -was a provision that the government should be consulted about the selling of these bonds. Have we ever heard anything as to these consultations and negotiations? If there were such, why have we not heard of them? The right hon. gentleman, so far as we know put the whole thing in the hands of a company that did not stand to lose one dollar whether the discount was 10 per cent or 20 per cent. I say it was a monstrous thing for any business government or any body of business men to put the country in that position.

I am sure the House is indebted to my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) for the information he has given in regard to the history of the Grand Trunk Pacific project. I do not know, however, that we can altogether appreciate what he is pleased to consider as the important features of that history. He has given us his recollections as to what took place, and his imaginings as to what may have taken place. May I trespass on the time of the House to say something about the same project from my point of view? First, let me say, there is no project so great that fault cannot be found with it in detail, and no project so good but some person can find something bad to say about it. So mv linn, friend has given us the benefit of his knowledge as to transactions within the Cabinet, private and confiden-

tial communications, and a large number of other matters which may be of importance to him and to those who are of his type of mind; but to my understanding these matters are not of importance as compared with the great question of the establishment of a Transcontinental railway in this Dominion and the results that necessarily follow, and have followed, and are following, the construction of that railway.	My hon.
friend has told us that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company made a proposition to the government for the construction of the railway from Port Simpson to North Bay. And he has told the House that, in his estimation, the country would have been better served if that project had been accepted. For my part, I would take issue with him and say that the country, in my opinion, would not have been as well served as by the present project; and will give my hon. friend some reasons for my belief. If the building of this road has any purpose at all, that purpose is the development of the prairie provinces, it is to enable the further development of these provinces as wheatgrowing areas and to provide means whereby the wheat grown in these provinces can reach the markets of the world by the most favourable route. I contend that the road from the prairies-say, froim Winnipeg taking that as a starting point-to Montreal, by way of North Bay, is not, and cannot in the nature of things, be as favourable a proposition for the development of the western country as a road of less length direct to the city of Quebec. A road which cuts out two hundred miles of haul between the wheat fields and the market is the better of the two propositions. I think that will not be denied.
Not necessarilj'' the best.
Mv hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) denies it.
And will prove it.

Does the bon. gentleman mean that the road is better because the country is paying the $10,000,000, and not the Grand Trunk Pacific?
. Mr. OLIVER. I mean to say that the road cost that money or it could not have been as good a road. Mr. Speaker, the Finance Minister has raised the curtain on another act of that comedy, or to speak with perfect truth, that tragedy of errors, whose successive acts ever since the opening m 1902 have followed with wearisome regularity and painful monotony. It certify is not a moral play, its best friends, if it has any outside the actors, and scene shifters, and box-office, would not say that the only interest in the play, outside the dazzling extravagance of the stageing, is in the fate of the actors, and the mystery that hangs round the future of the star actor, and the unhappy victims that have to finance the enterprise. Luckily, I believe, we must be coming to about the last act, for one cannot but notice that the actors other than the star have already vanished from the stage on which they have lagged superfluous far too long. The 'Star actor is apparently pacing ifrom one side to the other, calling the judgment of Heaven, or in other words, of the Privy Council, on the devoted heads of the Canadian people, whilst his .'faithful henchmen are urging him to seek a harbour of refuge m an alien port, which they are at the present time deliberately preparing for him.
Now, as I said, the curtain has been raised on what is apparently nearly the last act. Let us consider the position in which we are to-day. In my humble judgment there seems to be a complete misapprehension as to the judgment lately given by the Privy Council. I agree with every word that was said by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) this afternoon as to the duty of this House, the necessity with regard to the honour of the Canadian people, that we should bow to the judgment of the Privy Council. But one is so apt to be misunderstood, or even misrepresented, that I take the opportunity of saying that nobody, not even the magnates at the head of the Grand Trunk Pacific, bow more readily or humbly to that judgment than I do. But I do contend that there is an entire misapprehension as to the real meaning of that judgment, and so, like the hon. member for Hamilton, I shall certainly vote for this Bill because we think the government of this country should be placed in funds so that if it ever comes that, as honest and honourable men* representing an honourable country, we can fairly and properly be called on to pay $10,000,000, we should be in a position to do so. place to hear my appeal-I sincerely trust it will be many -a long day before the people of Canada will be victimized by paying the $10,000,000, which some people most wrongly have spoken of as a judgment against this country.

It must be admitted that, by the judgment of the Privy Council, accepting their construction of that clause, the meaning is that Canada is to implement-if I must reipeat that unhappy word which has cost us so much already-we must implement the guarantee of the bonds by paying in cash the amount which these bonds fall short. But supposing it were a covenant between the government and individuals. Supposing, instead of the government on the one hand and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the other, it was a case of a contract like that, and in order to make it perfectly plain, supposing it were a mortgage, or a covenant, between A and B, and B made default, I am willing to assume that Canada as represented by B made default, and that the mortgagee has a perfect right to call upon his mortgagor for payment, does it necessarily follow that the mortgagor must allow the judgment to go by default? Not at all. There may be a hundred defences he may have to his covenant, admitting that the covenant is there, and that, as a matter of strict legal interpretation, he is liable to the amount called for by _ the company. Let me illustrate. Supposing A has covenanted with B for $10,000 on a mortgage; B could say it is perfectly true, it is my covenant, and under that covenant I owe you $10,000, but you and I had a deal together in north west lands, and the result was that you have in your hands to-day $15,000 of my money, the result of our speculations in northwest lands. If B could prove that in his defence, does anybody pretend that a court would give judgment against him for $10,000? Far from it. The court would take the account between the two parties, and assuming that A owed the $10,000, if B owed him $15,000, then, by subtracting the 10 from the 15, the amount of the judgment for B against A would be $5,000.
