The land was obtained through the grossest deceit on the part of the representatives of this company and it is a breach of faith of the worst character that they should attempt to repudiate their contract. It is true that the time is not yet ripe for the construction of a station. The road is not built. It is not yet ready to open for traffic, hut an order may go requiring the Grand Trunk Pacific Bailway Company to construct and have ready for use by the public a station, the plans to he filed and approved by the Board's engineer, on lot 882, where it was intended originally to construct it. That station must be ready for operation at least as soon as the road is open for traffic.
An order may also go refusing the application that was filed with the Board on the 11th of December for the location of station grounds and a station on lot 851, and restraining the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company from the location of a station at that point. It is out of line with what they originally intended to do, done with bad motives, and it is done in violation of their solemn contract with the predecessor of Kelly in title.
Now, Sir, in quoting that language, I am not giving my own opinion, but the judgment of a judge, one of the principal judges in Canada, the Chief of the Railway Commission. My whole appeal now is that the country should not pay over this ten mifilions without investigation. Let us investigate first and pay, if necessary, afterwards, and not pay first and investigate afterwards. I think the wisest course for us is to investigate first. I have called attention to the action of the Grand Trunk Pacific magnates. It may seem to be going out of the way to attack an individual, but this whole country is concerned in what this individual is doing. Reputation will tell, and if a man is found under certain circumstances suspiciously situated, his reputation will help him out, or it may-ruin him entirely. Having said this much as to the way the country has been treated in the past, let me remind the House for a moment of two clauses in the contract. I presume I would not be wasting the time of the House if I were for a moment or two to refer to the fact that this was to be a Canadian road. It is so stated in the preamble of the first Bill, Chapter 91, 1903, and in the agreement made on the 29th of July, 1903, between His Majesty the King and Sir Rivers Wilson and other representatives of the Grand Trunk I find the following clause:
Whereas, having regard to the growth of population and the rapid development of the production and trade of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, and to the great area

of fertile and productive land in all the provinces and territories as yet without railway facilities, and to the rapidly expanding trade and commerce of the Dominion, it is in the interest of Canada that a line of railway, designed to secure the most direct and economical interchange of traffic between eastern Canada and the provinces and territories west of the Great Lakes; to open up and develop, the northern zone of the Dominion, to promote the internal and foreign trade of Canada and to develop commerce through Canadian ports, should be constructed and operated as a common railway highway across the Dominion from ocean to ocean and wholly within Canadian territory.
Clauses 42 and 43 of tlie contract also referred to the fact that it was to be a thoroughly Canadian road from ocean to ocean, with Canadian ports, and this is the ground upon which the government assisted the railway.
I think I need not occupy any more time to establish my chief proposition, that every 'dollar that this country has given to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway-and Heaven knows it has given mighty sums, and apparently will have to give mighty sums more-is based on an agreement that it was to be a thoroughly Canadian road, running from ocean to ocean wholly on Canadian soil, for the benefit of our inland commerce and our ocean ports.
I noticed in the month of August last that in the state of Massachusetts a railway charter was granted to some gentlemen, and I will read the names of the lucky men. I have here a copy of the charter, which is certified under the seal of the Commonwealth, so that for all practical purposes it i3 as good as the original. It reads thus:
The Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Be it known that whereas Charles M. Hays, Earl H. Fitzliugh, Ezra H. Baker

And a number of other names unknown to me, which I will not readand the Grand Trunk Railway Company -have associated themselves with the intention of forming a corporation under the name of Southern New England Railroad Corporation for the purpose of locating, constructing, maintaining and operating a railroad.
And they get their charter to build a railway through certain places in the state of Massachusetts. Now, there is at the present time a Bill before the House of Representatives of the state of Massachusetts, a copy of which I hold in my hand, entitled an Act to enlarge and extend the corporate powers of the Southern New England Railway Corporation, and, without going into details, I may say that thi3 Bill gives them the right to build a number of branch lines, among them one into Boston. It also authorizes the company to increase its capital stock to $10,000,000 and to issue bonds to twice the amount of the capital
stock actually paid in. So that these gentlemen, who are so hard up that they are coming to us for a loan of $10,000,000 to enable them to complete this road, are applying for power to increase the capital stock of this Southern New England Railway Corporation, for which they have obtained a charter, and to bond it to twice the amount of the capital stock paid in. Now, what is this road for? I confess that it is a mystery to me why our Canadian papers have not apparently been aware of what has been so frequently and conspicuously published in the Boston papers. I have here a file of the Boston papers, representing every paper published in Boston, and those papers for weeks and months past, day after day, have been full of this new enterprise to make Boston the Atlantic terminus of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I will not ask the House to take my word for this; I will read from some of these papers. But before doing so, let me say that the Senate of the state of Massachusetts has referred to a committee, which is to report not later than March 30, a number of questions which will enable the Senate to decide how far the Grand Trunk Pacific Company intends to make Boston its main port, and what advantage i't might he to the Commonwealth to acquire the property of any or all of the railways entering the city of Boston, and issuing bonds, &c., for that purpose. Let us see what the Boston papers themselves are saying about these matters. The Boston ' Globe ' of the 17th of January, 1912, says:
Plans of the Grand Trunk-Advantages offered to New England-Direct Rail Connection with Canadian Grain Country-Four Days from Boston to the Pacific.
Plans for bringing to the attention of the Massachusetts legislature the advantages to the state through the proposed extension of the lines of the Grand Trunk-Central Vermont system to Boston and Worcester are well under way.
E. H. Fitzhugh, president of the Central Vermont railroad and the recently chartered Southern New England railroad, and one of the chief assistants to Charles M. Hays, the American president of the Canadian Transcontinental railroad, came to Boston yesterday to meet the attorneys who will conduct the legislative hearings on the petition of the Southern New England railroad.
President Fitzhugh was in consultation yesterday afternoon and evening with lawyers, engineers and officers of the Central Vermont, who have been collecting the details concerning the proposed new line, which are to be submitted to the Committee on Railroads of tlie Legislature.
From the attitude of President Fitzhugh it is evident that President Hays is serious in his intention to build the line from Worcester, Vt., across New Hampshire and Massachusetts to Boston, to construct the branch from Boston to Blackstone and the crosscountry road from Douglas to Worcester as quickly as possible.

President Hays and President Fitzhugh are anxious that the railroads to Boston, Providence and Worcester be completed and ready for occupation by the time the last spike is driven on the Grand Trunk Pacific, now under construction from Moncton, N.B.t to Prince Rupert, B.C. Hundreds of miles east and west of Winnipeg are ready for operation, but it may be a couple of years before the long road across the continent is finished.
During this period of construction the Grand Trunk wishes to build the 130 miles or so that separate the Central Vermont at Windsor from a Boston terminal, in order that Boston may be one of the terminals of the railroad from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The purpose of the Southern New England railway, as will be argued before the committee of the legislature, is to give Boston and New England a direct rail connection with the great grain country of the Canadian west and northwest, to place the manufacturers of New England in touch with the market of the growing agricultural and purchasing sections of the Dominion.
The Grand Trunk railway through the Southern New England railway, is coming to Boston to bring business here and to create a. traffic between factories here and the prosperous communities that will be developed along the new transcontinental road.
The idea of President Hays is to stimulate commerce by adding Boston and the New England manufacturing centres to a line that will stretch across the continent and will he the longest railroad in the world under one management.
The Southern New England from Boston will be as much a part of the transcontinental trunk line as is the section of track which is now being laid across the Rocky Mountains in British Columbia.
It is for the purpose of shortening the distance from the New England factory to the farmer of western Canada and putting the manufacturer in touch with the purchaser on the same line of railroad that the Grand Trunk has applied for the authority to build a railroad to Boston and Worcester.
At the same time the Grand Trunk is seeking the traffic from the large manufacturing cities of New England to the British Columbian towns that are springing up as fast as the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific are laid. President Hays wishes to reach all the manufacturing centres of New England.
After speaking of the possibility of tapping the mill centres, the article goes on:
The bu'lding of the proposed Southern New England from Boston, upon the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, will mean the possibility of trains being operated from Boston to Princo Rupert, the Pacific terminus, in a running time of within four days.
The Grand Trunk Pacific is being built with an average grade as low as four-tenths of 1 per cent. The grade through the Canadian Rockies is as low as that across the plains, which will give to the Grand Trunk Pacific a train capacity of far greater tonnage than that of any other transcontinental road.
When the proposed railroads are completed a train running on the time now made by the Intercolonial Limited between Montreal and Mr. NORTHRUP
Toronto will cover the distance between Boston and Prince Rupert within four days. _ All of the construction is of the heaviest rails that are now rolled and there is not a wooden bridge on the road.
The Grand Trunk in extending its line to the Pacific has looked with particular favour upon the port of Boston and the mill cities of New England. President Hays thinks that a great deal of business for the new railroad across the continent may be developed in the territory to be tajoped by the Southern New England railway. The Grand Trunk has to make traffic for its transcontinental road and New England is considered to be an inviting field.
There is an editorial in the same issue of the Boston ' Globe ' headed ' Welcome, Grand Trunk.' I do not wish to occupy the time of the House by reading, as I might do, editorial after editorial on this matter. But I wish to refer to a long article in the Boston ' Sunday Herald ' of January 28, 1912, in which there is a map showing the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway running directly from Boston to Montreal, then to Scotia Junction, then to Cochrane, and then to Prince Rupert. Here is the great Transcontinental line, which we have been subsidizing to such a tremendous extent, going to Boston, and the Boston papers publishing maps showing its route from Boston to Prince Rupert over which the trip will be made in only four days. The heading of this article is: ' Linking Boston with the Far Pacific.' In the article there are two or three striking passages. It points out that when the railway is completed it will be possible for passengers and freight to make an uninterrupted journey from Boston to Prince Rupert, and then says:
This means such men of affairs as Chairman Hugh Bancroft of the directors of the port of Boston, President Hays of the Grand Trunk, Augustus S. Cobb, the physiographic expert, and others point out, that Boston is going to share heavily in the enormous development of the Canadian Northwest, to be one of the vital links in the commerce between Europe and that district, even a link in the trade of the three continents* When this huge transoceanic, transcontinental line of travel gets really under way, the traveller from Liverpool bound, say to Yokohama, need buy only two tickets, one at Liverpool and another at Boston.
And to such simplicity it is played for freight to make a journey of this length, 12,000 miles, that the shipper at Liverpool need put only a through tag on liis goods and away they go over the sea, then over land and over seas again to their destination-the nearest approach to an airline route that the wizards of transportation have yet conceived with certainty of realization. In these days of talk about the development of business in Boston generally and that of the port in particular, there is much material for thought in the approaching completion of this transcontinental railway from Boston to Prince Rupert.

Now, the Transportation Committee of the Boston Chamber of Commerce and the Worcester Board of Trade have both passed reports favouring the Grand Trunk extension to Boston on the ground that Canadian ports cannot furnish an outlet for the exports of the great northwest.
It seems that the Boston * American,' one of the Hearst papers in Boston, was the first to start the scheme by sending out. petitions signed by 100,000 people^ which it transmitted to President Hays, asking him to do what is being done now. I have here a copy of the Boston ' American,5 January 14, containing a large picture of President C. M. Hays. On Juno 26, President Hays, of the Grand Trunk Company wrote this letter to the editor of the Boston ' American
Dear Sir,-Mr, Warman has called my attention to your letter of June 1, and the box of signatures to the petition inviting the Grand Trunk to come to Boston.
All of us here appreciate very much the good offices of the Boston 'American' in securing this long list of petitioners; and I write to assure you of my personal appreciation of your efforts.
Then there is an interview with Mr. Hays, and this is what he said:
The London representative of the ' American' acquainted President Hays on the last day of April with all that was being done in the 'American' campaign. The 'American' sent President Hays a cablegram reporting progress. In the morning the ' American ' received this cablegram in reply:
To the Boston 1 American,' Boston, Mass.
When the Boston ' American ' petitions and the official resolutions referred to in your cablegram have been received by me to be placed before the Grand Trunk board of directors, I am certain the subject will be duly considered by that body.
To be placed before the Grand Trunk Board of Directors. The applicant for the charter is Charles M. Hays, with half-a-dozen other names, but the petition is to be laid before the Grand Trunk directors.
President Hays returned to Canada late in May, and just before the last Sunday in the month received a reporter for the 'American.' The ' American ' wanted a message for its readers, the great boxes of petitions were almost ready for shipment to Canada. Not yet ready to take the public into his confidence, President Hays sent a brief message, which was interpreted to he an admonition to New England to keep on working and to ' hold the fort.'
This is what President Hays said in the ' American' last May, in Montreal, just before the arrival of the petition of the ' American ' readers to ' come to Boston ':
The officers of the Grand Trunk railway are certainly very grateful to the people of Boston and the neighbouring section of New England for jthe display of confidence in our company. We could not well be otherwise.
The part your newspaper has taken, in the
matter of inviting us to Boston, is little short of amazing. 1 believe the very first person who met me in London, on my arrival from Plymouth, was a representative of the Hearst News service. He called upon me several times subsequently.
He told me-your representative in London -about the unanimous vote of the Massachusetts Senate, the Massachusetts House, and the Boston City Council; and assured him that I would place the resolution before our board of directors just as soon as the official records had come to me.
I have been away a month. To-day for the first time I saw the transcript of these votes. To-day .also, I received the letter of his honour the Mayor, and saw the statement of His Excellency the Governor. Yon tell me I am soon to have the petition of iOO.OOO New Englanders.
Such a testimonial as this would make any railroad man happy. It makes ine very happy. What shall I say to make New England happy?
I will say this. I will say that not only the original resolutions j>assed by your House of representatives, your Senate and your City Council, together with the letter of Mayor Fitzgerald and the statement of Governor Foss, but also the 100,000 petition of the 'American,' will go to London and be formally placed before our board of directors.
Moreover, I believe I can safely say, to Boston and New England, that these votes, these expressions, this request, will receive all the consideration-all the courteous consideration-to which they are entitled.
For myself, personally, I wish you would say to the people of New England that I fully and deeply appreciate the good-will back of this movement.
Without taking up the time of the House longer, I may say that for some time back, and at the present time, there is a wide spread movement in Boston, supported 'by the legislature, the senate, the Boston City Council, the mayor, the Chambers of Commerce, and Boards of Trade in neighbouring cities, all urging the Grand Trunk to come to Boston; their papers are full of articles all along the same line, that Boston is to be the terminus of the Grand Trunk Pacific line, when it will be only four days to Liverpool. Now, in view of that fact, in view of the express contract which was made between the Grand Trunk Pacific and this government, in view of the fact that the millions and millions that we have given to that company, were given with the understanding, and for the purpose of getting a road wholly over Canadian soil to Canadian seaports, I think I am justified in calling on the right hon. gentleman who leads the government, and calling on the Finance Minister, to pay heed to these facts, and I say to them it is their duty, before they pay over one dcllar of this money, to investigate and see whether there is a wilful and deliberate attempt to break the contract made by the Grand Trunk Pacific with this country.

If it be the case that all the people in Boston whose views are expressed here are in the right; if it be the case that the Grand Trunk Pacific is coquetting with Boston; if it be the case, as stated in one paper, that it would cost $10,000,000 for the Grand Trunk to construct its terminals in Boston; at this very time when this country is being asked for $10,000,000, it would be well for this government to see whether or not Canadian money is being poured into the coffers of the Grand Trunk Pacific to be poured out into Boston, or whether this country is to have an entirely Canadian road from sea to sea over Canadian soil. In conclusion I wish to say, in order to avoid any misunderstanding, that I do hot for a moment repudiate the judgment of the Privy Council; but I wish to impress on the House and the government the construction I give to this judgment, and I hope they will investigate, before paying a dollar to this company, to find out whether there is anything in any of these points I have raised. But if we find that this country has defences which, as between private individuals, would be ample defences and ample counter claims, so that no court would think of ordering one to pay the other a dollar, then I say the present ministry will fail in their duty, and will deserve to be ranged in the same class as the late ministry, if they fail to protect the people of Canada, as the late ministers so ignominiously failed to protect them.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance how much money at the present time the Dominion of Canada is liable for under the sale of these bonds by reason of the judgment of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The implementing obligation upon sales of bonds already made amounts to about $5,000,000. Any funds that are due by way of implementing must be paid into the bank to the credit of the Receiver General of Canada, in like manner as the proceeds of the bonds are paid into that bank to be disbursed upon certificates of the government engineer from time to time as construction proceeds.

That is practically the answer I desire. I knew something about the agreement, and about the legal situation when that agreement went through, and I had an idea of my own that the common legal gentlemen whom the government at that time were getting advice from, were wrong. I thought at that time, and I think at the present time, the Do min on of Canada should protect those bonds, and if necessary borrow money at 3 per cent to buy them.
The agreement, as I understand it, provided that the bonds should not be sold Mr. NORTHRUP.
without the concurrence of the Dominion government. Then, the Dominion government, whether it was a Liberal or a Conservative government, should have seen that those bonds were not sold below the price for which the Dominion government securities are sold. I think that at this moment the present government should protect the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and if necessary borrow the money to purchase the bonds with the 3 per cent guarantee, and then the government of Canada and the people of Canada would lose nothing because the bonds would be worth 100 cents on the dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The questions my hon. friend has raised have been very fully considered by the government. It has been suggested, and it is a thought that at once occurs to a financial man, that in order to save the amount of implementing on bonds sold in the future (because the others are sold, they a^re gone), if the government should purchase at par those bonds from time to time _ as required for the purposes of construction by the Grand Trunk Pacific they would then have the 3 per cent bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific and would save the difference between their selling price, say 80 net, and par.
Sure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not too sure, it requires some further consideration. There are $25,000,000 worth more of bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific to be sold. I would point out to my hon. friend that these are 50 year bonds from the present day, that they mature in 1962. Where my hon. friend is wrong is just here:	These
are 3 per cent bonds. My hon. friend says why not have the Dominion borrow at par, because it can issue its securities approximately at par, and buy in the 3 per cents, you would then have the 3 per cents and you would save the difference. What he has overlooked is this. The standard security of the Dominion of Canada is not a 3 per cent security, but a 31 per cent security. If we borrowed inoney on a 31 per cent basis, practically speaking, issuing our bonds at par or a little under, then if we bought the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific let us consider our position. On the one hand we would be paying out 31 per cent on the amount we had borrowed to take them up and on the other hand we would be getting 3 per cent only from the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds. In other words we would be losing half a point of interest. Putting it on a financial basis, Grand Trunk Pacific 3 per cent bonds on a 31 per cent basis, at 82 are equivalent to 31

per cent at about 94. In other words, the equivalent of the Grand Trunk bonds guaranteed by this government at, we will say, 82, is on a 3J per cent basis, about 94, between 93 and 94. The transaction would be this: The Dominion would issue its securities at or near i>ar and would take up the remaining bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and in doing it they would save, on the estimate I have made, about. 5 points, not 20 points, not the difference between 80 and par but the difference between the rate of 93 or 94, because that is the corresponding rate on a 3i per cent basis, and the price at which Dominion securities would sell; So on $25,000,000 of bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, if we took them up and paid for them at par, that is to say implementing as we went along, the government would save about $1,250,000, or possibly a little more. But let me point out two considerations to my hon. friend. In the first place, in 'order to do that the government would have to increase the National debt by an amount of $25,000,000. In the second fclace we should have to consider the desirability of holding as an investment, bonds of the railway company, it is true, guaranteed by the government. The situation is not essentially different from this, that this government at any time can tnake 5 points if it desires to do so by buying the bonds of any Canadian railway Company guaranteed by the Dominion feovernment standing at 93 or 94.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The Dominion to-day can issue its securities at about par and can turn around and buy on the London market Canadian Northern or any other securities on a 34 per cent, basis, now selling at about 93, and in that way, we could make the difference. The difficulties are these two: Is it wise to increase the National debt by $25,000,000 to helip out that transaction for the amount that would be saved and second, is it advisable to hold securities of the railway company, guaranteed as they are by the Dominion government.

Will you allow the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, guaranteed by the government, to be sold at 20 per 'cent, less than par, rather than have the Dominion government itself take them up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have said that that is a matter for very careful consideration on the part of the government, and it is under consideration by the government. There are no discoveries being made 'with regard to this matter. It is the most obvious thing in the world for
a financial man to say we can save the implementing by taking them up, but these considerations I have mentioned are important considerations and not the least important is the question of the desirability of the government holding those bonds with the interest maturing from year to year, that is bonds which they have purchased with the proceeds of their own securities. It is not true that you gave 20 points, because you must put the security <on the same basis as that on which the Dominion sells its securities.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it. the pleasure of the House to aeccipt the motion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there are no -other speakers, I shall say a few words in reply as the mover of this motion. My hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Nortli-rup) has brought up some very interesting points in connection with this maitter, all or nearly all of which have had my careful consideration. The Bill which I am introducing, enables the government to carry out the obligation, whatever it may be, on the Dominion arising under this agreement -of 1903, as Interpreted by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. My hon. friend has referred to the fact that bonds were sold at less than par and he raises the very interesting question as to whether, if those bonds were improvidently sold, there would not be a set-off.
Now I may say to him that that is a matter about which I have made, and am now making, very careful inquiries. The results of my inquiries to date have been these:	It is provided somewhere in the
statute or in the agreement that the bonds which have been sold from time to time were sold with the consent of the government; in other words that the government consented to the time of issue and the price of the securities. That, of course, is not conclusive. But it is a fact, I am advised, that my predecessor in office and the government of that day approved of the sale of these bonds from time to time as required. Now, while.these bonds appear to be selling at a very low price- at 80, a discount of 20, a very heavy discount-yet it must be born in mind, as I have pointed out originally that at the time the bonds were to be issued, it was thought that they would sell at par or nearly at par, but since that time there has been a fall in all high-grade low-interest bearing securites. Among these, as mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) this afternoon, are British Consols, which have fallen to 76 or 77, a very great fall indeed. The standard security to-day that is the Dominion's direct liability security, is about par,-there have been sales at 1001 recently. It is a fact, and a curious fact, that a guaranteed bond never sells as high as a bond that

gives a direct obligation. You would think that in the case of the Dominion, its guaranteed securities would sell at precisely the same price as a security giving its direct obligation to repay. But it is not so, and this is probably the reason; Under the law, one "f the most easily defeasable contracts is the contract of guarantee; and, though the wording of the instrument of guarantee generally states that, notwithstanding anything that may be done, the covenant of the guarantor is absolute, nevertheless guaranteed bonds will not sell within some points of as high a price as the bonds or debentures or securities which represent the direct obligations of the Dominion. Let me repeat to my hon. friend from East Hastings, that all the sales will be carefully checked, that is the sales which have taken place in the past will be carefully checked. And let me say to him further that I understand that the auditor of the Railways Department has checked the disbursements

(I am only giving what I am told, for I have not had time to verify it myself.) At all events, the hon. member may assume this, that before anything is paid out in respect of bonds which have been sold in the past, a careful accounting will be made with regard to the matters which he mentioned- as to commissions and as to whether the sales were in any way improvident. My own opinion is-I must be frank with the House-that these sales are not improvident. And for this reason: If you iput a 3 per cent bond of the Grand Trunk Pacific on a 3} per cent basis and check it up with a 3J per cent debenture or bond on the London market, you will find that there is just about a parity. Consequently, the real question that arises in my judgment is an accounting to find out what the net proceeds actually were, so that in paying the difference between the proceeds and par you are careful that the Dominion does not pay too much.
Now, we come to another point raised by my hon. friend, the cost of production and interest. In the trust mortgage se-. curing the interest on these bonds the expression ' Construction work ' is thus defined :	,
The said expression ' construction work5 in regard to the section in respect of which the same is used, shall also include any sum or sums of money paid or to be paid by the Pacific Company as interest

That is, interest is part of construction:

accruing, or about to 'accrue, during the
period of construction, as hereinafter defined, upon the bonds issued by the Pacific Company and guaranteed by the government under this mortgage

The expression ' period of eonsitnietion/ that is, the period during which this interest shall run, is defined in this section V, which is the one I have read:

speechtext:
Section 7. The expression 'period of construction * in section 5 of this article shall mean the period of time which shall elapse until the western division shall he completed under the provisions of the Transcontinental Railway Acts, or of any Act of parliament extending the time for completion, and the government shall fix the date of sncli completion by order in council accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1 am glad to have the hon. .member's opinion, because I know he has gone into the matter thoroughly. With regard to this money which is due, using the expression generally, to the iGran'd Trunk Pacific, of course this money was to be received and held in trust by the Receiver General of Canada, who is the Finance Minister, under the terms of the trust mortgage securing this issue. ,
How much Is the exact amount at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
According to the statement which I made to the House the other day, it amounts to $4,900,000. Now let us see how that is to he paid up. That money is not to be at once handed over by cheque to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and it has never been suggested that it is so to be dealt with. Section 3. All of the said bonds shall be so issued that the purchase price of any of such bonds (hereinafter referred to as ' the proceeds' of the said bonds), shall be paid by the purchasers thereof from time to time into the Bank of Atoutreal, the Canadian Bank of Commerce, the Merchants Bank of Canada, or such other bank or banks as the government may approve of (which are hereinafter collectively and distributively referred to as the 1 Bank '). That is, the proceeds of the bonds sold by (the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. And I have pointed out to my hon. friend from East Hastings, that these bonds which were sold from (time to time were

sold with the consent of the Minister of Finance of Canada. I have explained also -the hon. gentleman was not present at (the time-that there lias been an accounting, I understand as to the disbursements., and I 'believe itliere was a check by the auditor of the Railway Department. However, that is a matter, as I have said, which will engage my most -careful attention before the money is ipaid over. In other words, the interests of the Dominion in regard to that will be absolutely safeguarded so far as it is possible to- do so. I raised this question with respect to tire first clause relative to the appointment of one commissioner, as I felt it was necessary that we should be furnished with information, not only with respect to the work that remained to be done, but also with respect to the status of the commission. We were under some misapprehension, I know I was, as to who really constituted the commission at that time. We were told that certain members of the commission had sent in their resignation. Whether any of the resignations had been accepted we were not able to ascertain. I felt it important that we should know that. Before we take into consideration the question as to whether we should reduce the numbers of this commission from four to one, we should know the work yet to be done. When this matter was first under consideration by parliament, parliament determined the number of commissioners to whom should be entrusted the responsibility and the duty of the construction of the Transcontinental railway between Winnipeg and Moncton, and parliament, in its wisdom, entrusted that work to a commission composed of four men. Had the proposition been to entrust it to a commission of one man, I am sure parliament would have hesitated before taking action. When it is proposed to reduce that number to one man, it is necessary for us to have information as to what part of the work remains uncompleted. We have had that here to-night, and although I listened as closely as I could, I am not yet in possession of the information which I require. We must remember that when the Intercolonial was constructed it was placed in the hands of a commission, I think there were three commissioners, and they remained until the road was completed. Had there been

a proposition to change the number when the work was half or two-thirds completed, I do not think parliament would have consented to it. Now when two years* work remain to be completed, I think it is an amazing proposition to place upon tile shoulders of one man the responsibility of completing the work, and determining the final settlements of contracts. The work yet to be done involves most serious responsibility. I care not how able a man may be, it is not wise, it is not in the interest of the public to entrust this great work to one man alone. Subsequent to the request I made to my hon. friend for the information he has just brought down, I moved that there should be furnished to the House certain other information. I moved for information with respect to the proceedings of the commission from the day this government came into power to the present time, from the time of the resignation of the present chairman down to the time I made my motion. That information has not, yet been furnished. I do not think that this committee is in a position properly to consider the proposition involved in the first section. The committee may determine when it has all the information that one man is competent to carry on the work, and that it would be wise to entrust it to the responsibility of one man.
I do not think the committee is in a position to say whether or not that would be a wise course. If, in 1903, the then Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had proposed to place the construction of that line from Winnipeg to Moncton in charge of one commissioner, parliament would have hesitated and perhaps have declined to give its_ sanction to such a proposal, and it is quite a serious matter at this moment. While there is not so much work yet to be done and while it does not involve so many years' labour, yet the responsibility in the final winding up and completion of the work is, in my judgment, a very large percentage of the responsibility that was involved in the whole work at its inception and it would be a dangerous precedent to establish. We must go upon precedent in these matters. At the time of the construction of the Intercolonial railway the precedent established was a commission of three members. That perhaps was not so great a work as thi3 although for that period it was a very great work and meant much for the future of Canada. The precedent established by parliament on that occasion is certainly worthy of being followed on this. I do not know if my hon. friend had not confidence in the commissioners, he placed no imputation on the members of the Transcontinental Railway Board. If lack of confidence in the commissioners was the reason for his desire to

change the hoard, then it might have been well to consider the substitution of other gentlemen on the board, but it is quite a different proposition to wipe out the commission and place in the hands of one man the whole responsibility and the complete control of this great work including the final accounting with respect to contracts. It is a serious responsibility for any man to assume and it is a serious consideration for this parliament whether they are willing to entrust that responsibility to one man and to rely upon his judgment, I care not how great, how able or how well qualified he may be, from an administrative or engineering or other standpoint. There are involved decisions of great importance not merely to the railway but to the people of Canada who are looking forward to the completion of the railway as a work that will mean much for the future. We may differ with respect to its cost, indeed there were differences with respect to its advisability in the first instance. As to the character of the road that was proposed to be built there were those who favoured its construction as a government work and those who felt that the whole project should be entrusced to a private railway corporation; but parliament in its wisdom determined that it should be built but not operated as a government roal, that it should be built not by the Department of Railways as canals have been built for years, directly under the control of the minister, but by a commission, and parliament wisely determined that that commission should consist of four men. My hon. friend Will find out-I have not time mow to refer to and quote the records of the proceedings of the House-that a motion was passed calling upon him and his department and the Transcontinental Commission to furnish this information. And I ask my bon. friend in all seriousness and in all sincerity, to have the further progress of this Bill deferred until I, at least as one member of the committee having the right to *make the request, shall have an opportunity of perusing, not merely the information brought down by him, but also the [DOT]further information for which I have asked in the motion to which I have referred [DOT]and which information has been ordered by the House to be furnished by his department.
Can the hon. gentleman give me the date when that motion was carried?
I have not carried this in my memory, but I think it was on the 27th of January.
It was on the 26th January, page 297 of the Votes and Proceedings.

The motion was as follows:
For a copy of all minutes of proceedings, records, orders, instructions or other writings made and had, or given or authorized to be made, had or given by the Board of National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners,' from the date of the appointment of Mr. If. W. Leonard, as a member of the said board and chairman thereof, to the present date; also of all letters, telegrams, instructions or other documents made or had or passed, since the said appointment, by and between the Minister of Railways and Canals, or other members of the government, or by any person by authority of the government, and the said chairman of Board of National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners, or the secretary of said hoard; also of any orders in council relating to the appointment of an assistant chairman or an assistant to the chairman of said board, together with a copy of all letters, papers, instructions or documents relating thereto; as well as a statement of all payments of monies in the way of salaries or compensation made to the incumbent of the office of assistant chairman or assistant to the chairman of said board, and of all papers, letters or instructions made, written or received by the said minister or the said chairman, relating to or in any way connected with the payment or authorization of said salary or compensation.
It will be observed here that I have designated the gentleman as assistant chairman and then as assistant to the chairman, because when I first asked my hon. friend

the Minister of Railways and Canals with respect to the appointment as to whether Mr. Macpherson had been appointed assistant chairman, he said:	No, but that
he, or somebody, had been appointed as assistant to the chairman. I fail to see the fine point of distinction with respect to the difference in tire names. But, I ask for this information, and in all fairness 1 think I am entitled to it as a member of the committee if no one else is desirous to see it. I observe by the order in council that Mr. Macpherson has been appointed as assistant to tire chairman. I want no misapprehension as to the tenor of my remarks with respect to either the gentleman who occupies the position of chairman of the commission or the gentleman who occupies the position as assistant to the chairman. I believe that no better selection could have been made than has been made with respect to Mr. Leonard as chairman of the board, and from my knowledge of Mr. Macpherson I think he is entitled to a position of that great responsibility and even of greater responsibility, if my information with respect to him is correct, and if my observation is at all measurably near what it should be. But, it is only the information that I ask for, and I trust that my hon. friend will do me the justice to furnish it.

Mr. Chairman, there has been a tendency in this debate, and in preceding debates, for members on the other side of the House to be very voluble in their defence of this present commission. The astounding statement that the* minister has made to-night with respect to the cost of he National Transcontinental railway, in so far as the eastern portion is concerned, is enough without any further evidence to enable this House to decide that the sooner this commission is got rid of the better it will be for the country, and when we consider that we have a good man who understands railway building and that we will be far more likely to reach an end of this unparalleled expenditure without making any further blunders, my impression is that instead of continuing these commissioners, the quicker they get out the better it will be for the country. One member of the commission has resigned and he was wisely informed to do so. The others know that they had better do so as quickly as they possibly can before the country becomes thoroughly seized of the figures which the minister has laid before the House to-night. I wonder if members of the House realize the astounding statement that the minister laid before us tonight? It comes in srange contrast with the quotations which have been given from the right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and Mr. Fielding who,
some years ago, made the statement that this railway would post the people of the country $13,000,000, an amount which would be. met out of the surplus of a single year. Compared with the figures which we have here to-night the $13,000,000 which was originally mentioned, is a mere bagatelle. Let us look at these figures which the Minister of Railways has given us. This railway has cost up to date, $113,000,000 and it is now estimated that it will cost to complete $57,000,000 which will make an amount of $171,726,000. That will be the capital outlay as close as we can come to it now. That is only for the eastern section, without reference to the obligations we have undertaken on the line from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert, without respect to the guarantees we have given and without respect to the $10,000,000 that we are asked to make a present of to the Grand Trunk. This is only the cost of the portion of the line from Winnipeg 'to Moncton, and the total is $171,726,000. That is without any interest at all. We know that during the time that the road is being built and until the work is confpleted,. the interest has to be meit and we know that we have also to meet the interest for seven years thereafter. The interest to the date of completion will be $16,055,000 and, supposing it is completed by 1914 we still have seven years during which we will have to pay interest and that will give us $39,434,000 more. That brings the expenditure up to $227,215,000. If we add to that the betterments that will surely take place, it will amount to $7,885,000 more and if we take the interest on one-ninth of a year, which means that $900,000 must be added, we have the astounding sum of $236,000,000 as the cost of the railway from Moncton -to Winnipeg. That does not include the $14,000,000 or $15,000,000 that the Quebec bridge will cost. Contrast that with the statements that were .quoted this afternoon and it seems. perfectly astounding that these hon. gentlemen could be so far astray in their calculations.
Leit us see how our share is gbing to figure out. I could scarcely believe it after the quotations which were made from the speeches of the right hon. leader of the opposition and his Minister of Finance, who assured the House and the country repeatedly that $13,000,000 was all that the road was going to cost. To date the interest has been $16,055,000; seven years interest will amount to $39,434,000, and if, as in all probability will be the ease, we have to provide for an extra year's interest at least, 'it will mean an addition of $4,500,000; so that $60,000,000 'of interest is going to be .paid out 'by this country in connection with the road instead of the $13,000,000 we were told it would cost by the right hon. gentleman and his Minister of Finance, calculations which are not

within one-fifth of what the road is going to cost us.
Let us look for a moment at the Grand Trunk side of it, and, although I have only had an opportunity to glance at the figures, I think I can make the House see the magnitude of the undertaking. What is the position of the Grand Trunk in this matter? The Grand Trunk will have to pay interest on $171,726,000, on betterments $7,884,000, and oai three years interest, or, in all, about $201,710,000. That means that the Grand Trunk will have to carry a burden of interest of three per cent, on $201,000,000; that means they will have to carry a burden of $6,000,000 a year of interest or $3,300 interest per annum on every mile of that road from Winnipeg to Moncton. You talk about reducing the freight rates on the grain coming from the west on a railway that has got to carry an interest charge of $3,300 per annum for every mile of its line. How much do you think there would be left over to reduce the rates after working expenses are paid? I can tell you that the other railways in this country are laughing in their sleeves at the result of this enormous and colossal blunder on the part of the late government. They realize that this railway wall never be a factor in reducing freight rates, because they know there is not a railway in all Canada that can begin to carry an interest charge on one thousand eight hundred miles of road, where every mile of that railway on an average has cost $130,000 a mile. I do not. think .any hon. gentleman in this House ever heard of a railway staggering along under such a burden as that. Is that going to be any relief to the farmers of the west?
I	fail to see it. Except it be in one way, and that is that the Dominion of Canada step in and take a bigger share of the burden than they are carrying to-day, and if the Dominion is willing to do that it may possibly make it possible for that railway to be operated in such a way that it will be a relief to the west. But, when we think we are through with $60,000,000 we are again on the horns of a dilemma. We have to offer to relieve the Grand Trunk Pacific from a large portion of the burden they carry, which will increase that $60,000,000 very materially, or else we have got to let them stagger along alone under that burden, in which case there will never be a reduction of freight rates. Instead of wasting the time of the House in sympathy for that commission which has got the country into this tremendous expense, it is far better that we should pass this Bill and let these gentlemen requiesoat in pace; let them pass out of the public sight and be glad they are permitted to do so, and let us got down to one good, reliable railway building man and put him in charge

and say to him: Make the best you can out of the bargain, get us out of it as reasonably as you can, and finish the road as best you can. In the meantime, we will be glad to have a full impartial investigation that will try to find out where some of this $235,000,000 has gone.

My hon. friend (Mr. Ames) tries to make out that there can be no possible reduction of freight rates from the west on account of the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but there is just one feature of lit that he has taken good care not to mention, and that is, that when the Grand Trunk Pacific is completed it wii' be able to haul freight from Winnipeg to Montreal or from Winnipeg to the winter ports in the lower provinces, at less than one-half the cost that the same freight can be hauled for at the present time. That can be accomplished by the Grand Trunk Pacific owing to its low grades. Another point my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) has forgotten to mention is that when this road is completed the Grand Trunk Pacific Company will not have to spend millions and tens of millions of dollars, as the Canadian Pacific railway is doing now, in order to put the road in a position to compete on anything like even terms with other railways. It was stated the other day by some hon. gentlemen on the other side that the Canadian Pacific railway was only too willing to reduce freight rates, but they did not do so because while they could stand it the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern could not. There is absolutely no ground for a statement of that kind' I can show to the utmost satisfaction of this House that on many products that are being cairied by the Canadian Pacific railway in the west to-day they are charging very much higher rates than they did a few years ago, so tfiat instead of lowering the freight rates of late years, in many cases they have been putting them up. ' While the Grand Trunk Pacific has cost a good deal of money to build it must be remembered that when the road is completed it will be able to haul grain and other products at less cost than any transcontinental road either in Canada or in the United States. I have not the slightest doubt that wheu the Grand Trunk Pacific is completed it will be able to reduce the enormous freight rates that are in existence to-day and which are fifty per cent or a hundred per cent even, higher in the west than they are in the east. I believe the Grand Trunk Pacific will be able to do that, while rendering a good service to the country, and that it will earn money to pay the interest on its cost, although that cost has been heavy. I believe, Sir, that the Grand Trunk Pacific will be a great blessing to the western farmer and that it

will not have to ask the government for further aid.
On the portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific completed from Edmonton to Winnipeg are the freights any lower now than they are on the Canadian Northern or the Canadian Pacific railways?

The Grand Trunk Pacific will not lower their freight rates of their own volition any more than any other railway will, but they can be compelled to do so by the Railway Commission, and the freight rates will be cut down and they can still earn interest on the charges. On account of their low grades the Grand Trunk Pacific will be able to carry on one train four times or five times as much as can be carried on one train of the Canadian Pacific railway from the Pacific coast to Winnipeg. From Winnipeg to the Atlantic ports they have a four-tenths of one per cent grade, which means that an engine can haul on that road any load that she can start with on an absolutely level track.
Did the government in making the bargain with the Grand Trunk Pacific reserve any control over the freight rates?
Every road in Canada is under the control of the Railway Commission.
Only under the control of the Railway Commission?

The railways are under the control of the Railway Commission; the Railway Commission is under the control of the government; the government brought the Railway Commission into being and the government can dissolve the Railway Commission if they want to at any time. The Railway Commission is under the control of this government just the same as any other commission. Let no one run away with the idea that because the Grand Trunk Pacific cost more than it was expected it would, simply because they built a better road than they started out to build, that it is going in the end to have any ill effect on the freight rates, because the fact is that on account of it being a better road it will be able to haul freight at a less rate than any competing road.

May I ask that the Bill be allowed to stand over until we have looked into the figures brought down by the Minister of Railways. It must be apparent that it is impossible, after simply hearing the figures, to come to any conclusion with regard to them. I hope my hon. friend will have no objection to allow the Bill to stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am unable to see how the passing of this Bill depends so essentially upon any examination of these figures. So far as the figures are concerned, they only give the details of what has been stated here over and over again, that the road is at the present time about two-thirds completed. So far as the cost is concerned, there cannot be any doubt about that. However, if the consideration of the Bill, in the opinion of the right hon. gentleman, does involve an examination of these figures, and if we are to have an exhaustive discussion of all these statistics for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not, so far as the construction of this railway is concerned, it is to be placed under one instead of four, I am willing to accede to his suggestion although I cannot see the importance of it.	_

I quite agree with my hon. friend that the Bill itself
does not depend upon these figures; but the figures have to be discussed-my hon. friend will not deny us that privilege- and they might as well be discussed upon this Bill as upon any other.

I do not think the appointment of Mr. Macpherson has anything to do with the Bill. I am quite satisfied that the appointment of Mr. Macpherson was recommended by the chairman, and that the order in council was perfectly regular. I might say, for the information of the hon. gentleman who has taken exception to it, that there was no authority under the Act for the commission to buy a foot right of way. It was only last year that the late government passed an order in council giving them the authority, and the consequence is that the right of way is in a very bad mix-up. Mr. Mac-pherson is put in charge of right of way, and is held responsible for it. He is also at the head office when the chairman is away on the work, because I think it is most important not to tie the chairman down to the head office all the time. He should be out to see for himself whether the divisional and other engineers are performing their duties. But I have no objection to postponing the discussion, and
I	move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

Before we pass from the consideration of the Bill, I desire to call the hon. gentleman's attention to page 1,909 of ' Hansard 'where he is represented as having said:
Young asks-on the ground of having had no holidays, hut one out of the seven years he has been in office-for six months salary.
II	r. Mclsaac asks for three months, and Mr. Calvert resigns without any condition.
I understood the minister to say that Mr. Mclsaac had resigned without any condition and that Mr. Calvert had asked

for three months' salary. I wouid like the minister to correct this statement
I have not the letters here, but the facts were fresh in my memory when I spoke before.

Will the minister give us the information again?
Mr COCHRANE I will give you all the information you want.
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend ' The Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908,' by providing for the appointment of an additional Civil Service Commissioner, who shall have the salary of a Deputy Head of a department.-Mr. Borden.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It may be perhaps more convenient to have a general discussion 'on the Bill if the right hon. gentleman has no objection. At the moment, I would simply say that the reasons for introducing the proposed Bill are twofold. In the first place, I understand that some difficulty has been experienced in the operation of the Civil Service Commission from the very fact that it consists of only two members; for if these members are divided in opinion on some matter of more or less importance, no action can be taken, and some very awkward situations are likely to be created, and I think have been created, for that very reason. In the next place, it is hoped and expected that the operation of the Civil Service Amendment Act of 1908 will be extended as expeditiously as may be practicable to the outside service. I do not intend to suggest that that can be done at once. It will be done only after some investigation and some inquiry, but we hope to make progress in it from the very first, and in view of that extension of the operation of the Act, it is thought desirable for that reason also that there should be another member of the commission.

I do not intend to go into any general discussion of this measure at the present sitting, as I think that can very properly be deferred until the second reading of the Bill; but in the meantime may I ask my right hon. friend if it is the intention of the government to extend the operation of the Civil Service Act within the present session or during the present year? I understand that there are several officers in the outside service whom it will be difficult to bring within the scope of the Act; but there are, on the other hand, a good many who can be brought in. For instance, the officials Mr. KYTE.	j n * i
in the post offices, customs offices and inland revenue offices in large cities, might very properly be brought within the operation of the Act at once. With regard to extending it further to the service, I would not be prepared to offer any suggestion now; I am quite aware that it is a matter of great difficulty. It may not be so very easy to apply the Act to the service of the different departments ill the country districts. With regard to the other point mentioned by my right hon. friend, it is not perhaps outside of the possibilities of human nature that two coinmissioners might not always see eye to eye. I have not known, however, that a deadlock has occurred except in very minor circumstances. It appears sometimes that on legal questions the commissioners have to refer to the Department of Justice. I offer no suggestion, I merely make this remark.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In reply to the right hon. gentleman, he will realize that as we were obliged to meet parliament within four or five weeks after assuming office, there has not been much opportunity, at least so far as I am concerned, to make any effective study of the matter he has mentioned. He has asked whether the Civil Service Amendment Act would be extended to certain officials in the outside service during the present session. I would not like to say at the moment that we will find time to make even the investigation that would be necessary for that purpose. He has asked whether its operations may be extended during the present year to some portion of the outside service. I would hope, and indeed I believe, that it will be possible to do so during the present year; but it will be impossible to pronounce at the present anv opinion as to how far that would be practicable. I would like, however, to have it understood that it is our desire and intention to proceed along that line so far as it is practicable.

There is no question that the Civil Service Amendment Act introduced by the ex-Minister of Agriculture was a great relief to public men. Until then ministers were pestered from morning to night by applicants, and they were very many. That amendment gave great relief to ministers, and allowed them to do some work in their offices. Now, to extend the principle to the outside service would be a further relief. I am quite sure that when my right hon. friend visits Montreal or Halifax on public business, he is besieged by a troop of applicants for public office. I do not see any reason why the same rule which applies to the inside service at Ottawa should not be applied to the other large cities of trie Dominion.

I do not agree at all with the remarks of the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux). You cannot
apply the Civil Service Act to the outside service as it is applied in Ottawa. I have one instance in my mind now in the county of Welland. A postmaster has been dismissed very lately, a young man, active, intelligent, acceptable to all the people of the locality, from the post office. His name is Mr. Buck. He kept the post office at Crystal Beach, in the township of Bertie, in the county of Welland; he was dismissed, .and a Mr. Rebstock was appointed in his place, who is a United States citizen. I want to call the attention of this government to the fact that they dismissed a Canadian citizen, who is not a partisan at all, who never took any part in politics except to vote as an intelligent man should, and that is for me, and they have appointed a young man of good ability, but a citizen of the United States, to that position. Now that young man wanted the position several years ago, and I refused to recommend him, because he was a United States citizen. But these hon. gentlemen, who were so much afraid of being tied up to the United States in a reciprocity agreement, have appointed a United States citizen as postmaster. I would like the Postmaster General to be here. I hope his colleagues will call his attention to the wrong that he has done. They did dismiss one postmaster in the county; I was not so much dissatisfied with that, because I dismissed a Conservative, and had him appointed. Now, I am frank to say that it is a serious problem to apply the Civil Service Amendment Act to the outside service. I doubt very much if it can be worked out. You may, by your Civil Service Commission, Tegulate the appointment of officers in the inside service, as in Ottawa, and probably in Toronto. But when you take it over the country generally, to whom will the commissioners who havp to make the appointments, apply for information? They will apply to the men who are the leading men in the locality, and the leading men in the locality will be the men who represent the constituencies, or the men who have endeavoured to represent the constituency. The commissioners will take their opinions from these men; if they do not do that, what will they do? You cannot appoint men strictly on examination. You may get good men who will pass excellent examination, and who may be-absolutely unfit for public positions, from disposition, from character, or other inability. You cannot appoint young men simply by reason of the fact that they
have passed a first-class examination. I venture to say, and I want to say now in the presence of the hon. gentlemen who are leading this government, that we have in the county of Welland the best contingent of customs officers and immigration officers that exist in the Dominion of Canada.
I stand in the judgment of the commissioner of Customs and of. the Commissioner *f Immigration. They are all young men, they are all intelligent men, and I will put them up against any similar class of young men in the inside service who have !been appointed by your commissioners. They are intelligent, good young men, I do not want to see them dismissed and I do not expect they will be dismissed because they should not be dismissed. They may dismiss a few labourers on the Welland canal but I hope not many. The government cannot appoint a Civil Service Commission who can satisfactorily control the appointment of outside officials; if they undertake it they will make a mistake. It should be left to the men in the various counties in whom the government have confidence. If these men do not make proper representations to the government and the government have no confidence in them, then the government should select someone in whom they have confidence and be guided by his advice, even in the county of Welland, if they happen to be guided by mine.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know anything of the cases to which my toon, friend has alluded, but I shall bring his remarks to the attention of the Postmaster General.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and agreed to.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
